vignette: The night it happened, the argument in their shared apartment had spiraled past words into heavy, sudden violence. When the door finally gave way, his partner dragged him onto the sidewalk and pressed him against the metal frame of a bus shelter. The glass was cold and unyielding against his ribs. He felt the heavy grip on his shoulders, the hot breath near his ear, the whispered threats about what would happen if he tried to leave. The rumble of a passing bus vibrated through the shelter, shaking the exact spot on his collarbone where fingers had dug in. Minutes later, sirens cut through the tension, but the moment did not end when the police arrived. It settled into him. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that people could not be trusted, and that he was inadequate for surviving it without more force. He would sit in quiet rooms long after the noise had faded, dwelling on what he had done wrong, analyzing his tone, his posture, his choices, certain that if he had only acted differently, the violence would never have reached this point. The memory did not arrive as a photograph. It arrived as a re-entry. When the smell of diesel fuel hit his nose, or when a heavy hand accidentally brushed his shoulder in a crowded café, his body would instantly return to the shelter. His vision would tunnel, his chest would tighten, and the exact spot on his collarbone would throb with a sharp, familiar pain. He could not sit through the wave. The emotion would crest so fast he had to step away, grip the edge of a table, and wait for the air to return. What frightened him most was the certainty that the memory was not over; it was happening right now, and the threat was still present. His days became a series of quiet checks and deliberate silences. He would wake during the night, heart hammering against his ribs, and pad through the apartment to verify the locks, the window, the darkness. Even when his girlfriend, Mei, found him pacing at three in the morning, wrapping her arms around his back and insisting he was safe, the words landed on him like water on stone. He loved her, but even when others told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe it. The fear of harm had become a constant compass. A missed train, a delayed meeting, a text that went unanswered-each pause felt like a crack in the floor. He would assume something bad was happening, his mind already rehearsing worst-case scenarios. He had come to believe that you can never know who will harm you. Alongside the sleepless nights and the constant scanning, Thong had developed a quiet routine of physical and emotional restraint. He avoided eating, restricting his food to small portions of broth or skipping meals entirely. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger, fearing it would make him unpredictable or unworthy. At work, as a journalist covering municipal transit and public safety, these habits hardened into professional distance. When a male editor requested a follow-up interview in a private back office, Thong would politely decline, citing scheduling conflicts. He began taking the subway to avoid the bus, though the underground tunnels sometimes sparked the same frantic checks. When he did ride the bus to cover a city council meeting, he would sit near the doors, knees locked, eyes fixed on the passing poles, watching the other male passengers with a quiet, exhausting vigilance. The turning point came on a Tuesday in October. He had agreed to attend a press briefing downtown, but when a male source began walking beside him down the hallway, placing a hand on his shoulder, Thong felt his breath vanish. He stepped away, muttered an excuse, and left the building. Walking to the bus stop, he realized he could no longer ignore the architecture of his own days. He sat on a bench outside a community clinic, the weight of six months of isolation, skipped meals, and fractured sleep pressing down on him. He wanted to sleep through the night. He wanted to read his notes without his hands shaking. He was afraid of the next confrontation, but more than that, he hoped someone might help him untangle the belief that he was still standing in that bus shelter. He had finally dialed the number for trauma-informed therapy.
